A Visual Analytics Study of a Motor Insurance Portfolio

Wang Xiaohan

2026-05-21

This executive summary investigates what drives the profitability and volatility of a Spanish motor insurance portfolio. The analysis moves from describing how losses are distributed, through statistically testing candidate factors, to a multivariable model and a fair-comparison funnel plot, ending with concrete underwriting implications.

The Business Question

“Insurers often carry underperforming portfolios where the root causes of poor profitability and high volatility are unknown.”

  • 105,555 policy-year records, 30 variables (Spain, 2015–2018)
  • No ready-made profitability field → I derive the Loss Ratio (claims / premium); above 100% = a technical loss
  • Goal: statistically validate the factors influencing profitability and volatility

The portfolio contains over 100,000 policy-year records across 30 variables. Because the dataset has no ready-made profitability field, the central metric — the Loss Ratio, claims divided by premium — is derived during data preparation. A value above 100% indicates a technical loss. All subsequent analysis revolves around explaining this measure.

How Losses Are Distributed

  • 81% of policies have no claim (Loss Ratio = 0)
  • Among claiming policies, median Loss Ratio stays below 100% (break-even)
  • A long right tail exceeds break-even; the 800% cap holds catastrophic policies
  • Profitability is driven by the tail, not the typical claim

About 81% of policies have no claim at all. Among those that do, the Loss Ratio is strongly right-skewed: most stay below the 100% break-even line, but a long tail runs at a technical loss. The spike at the cap represents catastrophic policies whose losses exceed eight times the premium. Profitability is therefore driven by the tail, not the typical claim.

Do Vehicle Types Differ?

  • All four vehicle types share a similar peak near Loss Ratio = 0
  • Motorbikes & vans show heavier right tails than agricultural
  • Quartile colours show wide spread (Q4 reaches the cap)
  • Shapes look distinct — but is the difference statistically real?

The ridgeline plot compares Loss Ratio distributions across the four vehicle types, with fill encoding quartiles. Motorbikes and vans show heavier right tails than agricultural vehicles. These shapes look visually distinct — but as the next slide shows, that visual difference does not survive a formal statistical test.

A Formal Test Says: No

  • Kruskal-Wallis χ² = 2.31, p = 0.32 (not significant)
  • Median Loss Ratios close: Motorbike 0.60, Van 0.64, Car 0.76
  • Vehicle type does not affect claim severity
  • → Redirect the search to claim frequency

A Kruskal-Wallis test returns p = 0.32, well above 0.05. Despite the visually distinct ridgeline shapes, vehicle type does not significantly affect claim severity once a claim has occurred. This negative result is important: it redirects the search for drivers away from severity towards claim frequency. Honest reporting of a non-significant result reflects sound statistical practice.

The Large-Sample Trap

  • Chi-square χ² = 86.4, p = 1.5e-20 (highly significant)
  • But Cramer’s V = 0.03 → negligible association
  • Real gap is tiny: 18% (rural) vs 20% (urban)
  • With 105,555 rows, trivial gaps turn significant
  • → Effect size matters, not just the p-value

The chi-square test is highly significant, suggesting area matters. But the effect size, Cramer’s V, is only 0.03 — negligible. The actual gap is just 18% rural versus 20% urban. With over 100,000 records, even a trivial difference becomes statistically significant. Reading the p-value alone would mislead; the effect size shows area is not a material driver.

No Strong Numeric Predictor

  • Vehicle attributes are highly intercorrelated: Value–Weight 0.87, Cylinder–Value 0.79
  • Claim cost correlates weakly with all factors (|ρ| ≤ 0.09)
  • Premium tracks vehicle attributes (0.39–0.44), not actual loss
  • No single variable predicts loss → risk is idiosyncratic

The heatmap shows two things. Vehicle attributes are highly intercorrelated — value, weight, power and cylinder capacity all measure the same underlying size. More importantly, claim cost correlates only weakly with every factor. No single numeric variable predicts loss; risk in this portfolio is largely idiosyncratic, which is why a multivariable approach is needed.

A Fair Comparison: The Funnel Plot

A funnel plot object with 8 points of which 2 are outliers. 
Plot is adjusted for overdispersion.
  • Small segments (e.g. agricultural, ~850 policies) fluctuate by chance
  • Agricultural sits deep inside the funnel → noise, not signal
  • 2 of 8 segments fall outside the limits → genuinely unusual
  • Largest segment (cars, ~60,000) lies on the mean line → stable
  • Adjusted for overdispersion (extra-Poisson variation)

The funnel plot reframes the comparison correctly. The two agricultural segments sit far left with very low exposure — a naive ranking would call them the safest, but their position inside the wide funnel shows this is noise, not signal. Two segments fall outside the control limits and are genuinely high-risk. The largest segment lies on the mean line, confirming stability. The plot adjusts for overdispersion, appropriate for insurance claims.

What Really Drives a Claim?

  • Vehicle type is the one robust driver of claim incidence
  • Vans & cars have OR < 1 → lower odds than motorbikes
  • Numeric factors (age, value, power) cluster at OR ≈ 1 → little effect
  • Agricultural OR ≈ 100 but CI > 1,000 → small-sample noise
  • Funnel plot & model cross-validate each other

The forest plot delivers the clearest answer. After controlling for all factors, vehicle type is the one robust driver: vans and passenger cars have significantly lower claim odds than motorbikes. Numeric factors cluster around an odds ratio of one. Agricultural vehicles show a huge odds ratio but an extremely wide confidence interval — an unreliable small-sample estimate, exactly the artefact the funnel plot warned against. The two methods cross-validate each other.

Key Findings and Implications

Profitability is concentrated — about 91% of policies are individually profitable, yet a small catastrophic tail (Technical Result down to −€260,000) dominates the portfolio’s economics. Managing the tail matters more than average pricing.

No single factor predicts loss — vehicle type (Kruskal-Wallis p = 0.32), area (Cramer’s V = 0.03), and vehicle value (Spearman ρ = 0.13) are all statistically weak or negligible. Risk is largely idiosyncratic.

Structure lies in frequency, not severity — after controlling for all factors, vehicle type is the one robust driver of whether a claim occurs (vans & cars OR < 1). The apparent “agricultural risk” (OR ≈ 100, CI > 1,000) is small-sample noise, cross-validated by the funnel plot.

Three recommendations:

  1. Manage the tail policies, not across-the-board rates
  2. Compare segments by exposure, not raw claim rates
  3. Pursue data enrichment — current rating factors miss true risk

The evidence converges on a coherent picture. Profitability is concentrated in a catastrophic tail. No single variable strongly predicts loss — all candidate factors are statistically weak or negligible. Where structure exists, it lies in claim frequency, driven by vehicle type, not severity. Three underwriting recommendations follow: manage the tail rather than raising all rates, compare segments by exposure, and pursue data enrichment because current rating factors capture the vehicle’s physical characteristics far better than its true risk.
